questions.stem: A DNA nucleotide is made of three components. Which list names them?
options: A deoxyribose sugar, an amino acid and a phosphate group
A phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, a ribose sugar and one amino acid side chain
A glycerol molecule, a fatty acid and a nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: Each DNA nucleotide has a phosphate group, the sugar deoxyribose and one of four bases (A, T, C or G). Ribose is the sugar in RNA, and amino acids are the units of proteins.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes complementary base pairing in DNA?
options: Adenine pairs with guanine and cytosine pairs with thymine
Adenine pairs with uracil and cytosine pairs with guanine
Adenine pairs with cytosine and guanine pairs with thymine
Adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine
questions.explanation: In DNA, A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G, held together by hydrogen bonds. Uracil replaces thymine only in RNA.

questions.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence ATGCCGTA. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
options: GCATTACG
TACGGCAT
ATGCCGTA
UACGGCAU
questions.explanation: Each base is replaced by its partner: A with T, T with A, G with C and C with G, giving TACGGCAT. A sequence containing U would be RNA, not DNA.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 30%, making 60% in total. The remaining 40% is split equally between cytosine and guanine, so guanine is 20%.

questions.stem: During DNA replication, what is the role of helicase?
options: It adds new nucleotides to the growing DNA strand
It joins the separate sections of new DNA into one long strand
It makes a short primer where copying can begin
It unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands
questions.explanation: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, unwinding and separating the strands so each can act as a template. Adding nucleotides is the job of DNA polymerase, and joining sections is done by ligase.

questions.stem: Which enzyme adds complementary nucleotides to build a new DNA strand during replication?
options: Primase
DNA polymerase
Helicase
RNA polymerase
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase reads the template strand and adds free nucleotides with complementary bases to the new strand. It can only extend an existing chain, which is why a primer is needed first.

questions.stem: Why is primase needed before DNA polymerase can begin copying a template strand?
options: DNA polymerase needs primase to supply it with energy
DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing primer
Primase unwinds the strands so that DNA polymerase can bind
Primase seals gaps in the sugar-phosphate backbone of new DNA
questions.explanation: Primase makes a short primer that provides a starting point; DNA polymerase then adds nucleotides onto it. Unwinding is done by helicase and sealing gaps by ligase.

questions.stem: After DNA polymerase has finished copying, separate sections of a new strand still need to be joined into one continuous strand. Which enzyme does this?
options: Primase
Endonuclease
Ligase
Helicase
questions.explanation: Ligase forms bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, joining sections of DNA into a continuous strand. Endonucleases do the reverse, cutting DNA.

questions.stem: What does the term 'semi-conservative replication' mean?
options: Half of the original DNA is broken down and replaced each time
Each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one new strand
One new DNA molecule is all original and the other is all new
Each strand of new DNA is a random mix of original and new pieces
questions.explanation: In semi-conservative replication each original strand acts as a template, so each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand and gains one new strand. The model in which one molecule is entirely original is conservative replication.

questions.stem: Bacteria grown on heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) are moved to light nitrogen (¹⁴N). After two rounds of replication, what DNA would semi-conservative replication predict?
options: Half intermediate density and half light
All of intermediate density
One quarter heavy and three quarters light
Half heavy and half light
questions.explanation: After one round every molecule is hybrid (one ¹⁵N and one ¹⁴N strand). In the second round each hybrid gives one hybrid and one all-light molecule, so half are intermediate and half light. This was the result Meselson and Stahl found.

questions.stem: Why is semi-conservative replication significant for living cells?
options: It ensures each daughter cell receives different alleles
Each original strand is a template, so copies are accurate
It allows new genes to be added to the DNA at each division
It lets the cell use half as many nucleotides per division
questions.explanation: Because each strand serves as a template for complementary base pairing, the two new molecules are almost exact copies. This lets genetic information pass accurately to daughter cells.

questions.stem: Which enzymes are used to cut DNA at specific base sequences?
options: Restriction endonucleases
DNA ligases
Heat-stable DNA polymerases
RNA polymerases
questions.explanation: Restriction endonucleases recognise particular short sequences and cut the DNA there. Ligases join DNA, and polymerases build new strands.

questions.stem: To make recombinant DNA, a gene and a plasmid are cut with the same restriction enzyme and then mixed. Which enzyme joins the gene into the plasmid?
options: Helicase
Primase
Endonuclease
DNA ligase
questions.explanation: Cutting both with the same enzyme gives matching ends that pair up. DNA ligase then seals the sugar-phosphate backbone, joining the gene permanently into the plasmid.

questions.stem: In the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which enzyme synthesises new copies of the target DNA?
options: A heat-stable DNA ligase
Helicase from bacteria
A heat-stable DNA polymerase
A restriction endonuclease
questions.explanation: PCR copies DNA in repeated cycles of heating and cooling. A heat-stable DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to primers to build new strands; heat, not helicase, separates the strands in each cycle.

questions.stem: What is genome sequencing?
options: Counting the chromosomes in a cell during division
Joining genes from two species into one DNA molecule
Finding the order of nucleotides in an organism's DNA
Cutting an organism's DNA into a set number of genes
questions.explanation: Genome sequencing determines the order of the bases A, T, C and G across an organism's DNA. Joining genes from two species describes making recombinant DNA.

questions.stem: Which is a use of genome sequencing in biology and medicine?
options: Identifying mutations that are linked to genetic diseases
Making all of an organism's genes identical to one another
Converting the introns in DNA into working exons
Stopping mutations from occurring in future generations
questions.explanation: Comparing sequences between people lets scientists find mutations associated with disease and design tests or treatments. Sequencing reads DNA; it does not change it.

questions.stem: What are introns?
options: Coding sections of a gene that are joined together in the mRNA
Sections of mRNA that bind to the ribosome during translation
Short sequences that tRNA molecules use to attach and carry amino acids
Non-coding sections of a gene, removed from mRNA before translation
questions.explanation: Introns are non-coding regions within a gene. They are transcribed but then removed, and the coding regions (exons) are joined to form mature mRNA.

questions.stem: Where do transcription and translation take place in a eukaryotic cell?
options: Both take place in the mitochondria of the cell
Transcription in the nucleus; translation at ribosomes
Transcription at ribosomes; translation in the nucleus
Both take place in the nucleus of the cell
questions.explanation: DNA stays in the nucleus, where a gene is transcribed into mRNA. The mRNA travels to ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where it is translated into a sequence of amino acids.

questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads TAC CGT AAA ATC. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
options: AUG GCA UUU UAG
ATG GCA TTT TAG
TAC CGT AAA ATC
UAC CGU AAA AUC
questions.explanation: mRNA is complementary to the template strand, with uracil in place of thymine: T gives A, A gives U, C gives G and G gives C. A sequence containing T would still be DNA.

questions.stem: An mRNA codon is GCA. What is the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it?
options: CGU
GCA
CGT
UGC
questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary to the codon, using RNA bases: G pairs with C, C with G and A with U, giving CGU. Thymine is not found in tRNA.

questions.stem: Using AUG = methionine, GCA = alanine, UUU = phenylalanine and UAG = stop, which amino acid sequence does the mRNA AUG GCA UUU UAG code for?
options: Methionine, alanine, phenylalanine, stop amino acid
Alanine, phenylalanine, methionine
Phenylalanine, alanine, methionine
Methionine, alanine, phenylalanine
questions.explanation: Ribosomes read codons in order from the start codon: AUG, GCA, UUU. The stop codon UAG codes for no amino acid; it ends translation, releasing the chain.

questions.stem: The coding part of an mRNA, from the start codon up to and including the stop codon, is 450 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
questions.explanation: 450 nucleotides make 450 ÷ 3 = 150 codons. The stop codon does not code for an amino acid, so the polypeptide has 149 amino acids.

questions.stem: What is the role of tRNA in translation?
options: It carries the genetic code from the nucleus to the ribosome
It joins the two strands of DNA back together after transcription has finished
It forms the bonds between neighbouring codons on the mRNA
It carries a specific amino acid and matches its anticodon to a codon
questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries one kind of amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a matching mRNA codon, so amino acids are added in the right order. mRNA, not tRNA, carries the code from the nucleus.

questions.stem: In the lac operon of E. coli, what happens when lactose is absent?
options: RNA polymerase binds to the repressor to start transcription
A repressor binds to the operator and blocks transcription
Lactose binds to the operator and switches the genes on
The structural genes are transcribed at their highest rate
questions.explanation: With no lactose, the repressor protein binds the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes. The cell does not waste energy making enzymes it has no use for.

questions.stem: Lactose is added to E. coli growing without glucose. Why are the enzymes for lactose use then made?
options: Lactose binds the repressor, which leaves the operator free
Lactose binds the operator, which attracts RNA polymerase
Lactose destroys the gene that codes for the repressor
Lactose acts as the template for making the enzymes
questions.explanation: Lactose (as allolactose) binds the repressor and changes its shape, so it can no longer bind the operator. RNA polymerase can then transcribe the structural genes, and the enzymes for taking up and breaking down lactose are made.

questions.stem: In the lac operon, which gene product controls whether the structural genes are transcribed?
options: The enzyme that breaks down lactose
The mRNA made from the structural genes
The tRNA that carries the first amino acid
The repressor protein from the regulatory gene
questions.explanation: A regulatory gene codes for the repressor protein, which switches the operon off by binding the operator. The structural genes code for the enzymes, which do not control their own transcription in this model.

questions.stem: A muscle cell and a nerve cell from the same person contain the same genes, yet have very different structures. Why?
options: Mutations have changed the genes in each cell type
Different genes are expressed in each cell type
Each cell type has lost the genes it does not use
Each cell type has a different set of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Cells differentiate through differential gene expression: different genes are switched on and off, so each cell makes different proteins. The genes themselves are the same in almost every body cell.

questions.stem: Siamese cats have dark fur on their ears and paws but pale fur on their bodies. The pigment enzyme works only below body temperature. What does this show?
options: Cold temperatures cause mutations in the pigment gene
Fur colour is controlled by several unlinked genes
The environment can affect how a genotype is expressed
The ears and paws carry different genes for fur colour
questions.explanation: All the cat's cells carry the same pigment allele, but the enzyme is active only in the cooler extremities. The phenotype therefore depends on both genotype and environment, not on different or mutated genes.

questions.stem: Why can the product of one gene affect the phenotype controlled by another gene?
options: Each gene codes for the base sequence of the next gene along the chromosome
Genes swap their exons with each other during translation
Every gene shares a single mRNA with its neighbouring gene
Proteins such as enzymes and regulators act on other genes' pathways
questions.explanation: Many phenotypes depend on a pathway of several enzymes, and some proteins regulate the transcription of other genes. A faulty product from one gene can therefore change what another gene's product achieves.

questions.stem: Which description fits a point mutation?
options: A change affecting a large block of genes
A change to the sequence of amino acids only
A change to a single nucleotide in DNA
A change to the number of chromosomes
questions.explanation: A point mutation alters one nucleotide, for example by substitution, addition or deletion of a single base. Changes to large segments of chromosomes or to chromosome number are block and chromosomal mutations.

questions.stem: A substitution changes the codon GAA to GAG, and both codons code for the same amino acid. What is the effect on the protein?
options: A shorter protein, because GAG is a stop codon
A frameshift, changing every amino acid that follows the altered codon
A longer protein, because an extra codon is added
No change, because the code has more than one codon per amino acid
questions.explanation: The genetic code has several codons for most amino acids, so this substitution is silent and the protein is unchanged. Only additions or deletions shift the reading frame.

questions.stem: Which mutation near the start of a gene is most likely to make the protein non-functional?
options: Substitution of one nucleotide
Deletion of three adjacent nucleotides
Substitution at the third base of a codon
Deletion of one nucleotide
questions.explanation: Deleting one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is changed and a stop codon often appears early. Deleting three bases removes one amino acid but keeps the frame, and a single substitution changes at most one amino acid.

questions.stem: A substitution changes the codon UAC (tyrosine) to UAG (stop) in the middle of a gene. What is the likely effect?
options: A protein that is longer than normal
A shortened protein that probably does not work
A protein with one different amino acid only
A protein with every later amino acid changed
questions.explanation: A substitution that creates a stop codon ends translation early, so the polypeptide is incomplete and usually non-functional. A change to one amino acid would occur only if the new codon coded for a different amino acid.

questions.stem: What is an inversion mutation?
options: A section of DNA is turned around end to end
A section of DNA is copied and added again
A section of DNA is lost from the chromosome
A section of DNA moves to a different chromosome
questions.explanation: In an inversion a segment breaks out and is reinserted in the reverse orientation. A copied segment is a duplication, a lost one a deletion, and one moved to another chromosome a translocation.

questions.stem: Errors in separating chromosomes during cell division can produce a gamete with an extra chromosome. What type of mutation results in the offspring?
options: A frameshift mutation within a single gene
A chromosomal mutation that changes chromosome number
A point mutation that changes one nucleotide
A silent mutation that has no effect on proteins
questions.explanation: When chromosomes fail to separate, a gamete may gain or lose a whole chromosome, so the offspring has an abnormal chromosome number, as in trisomy 21. Point and frameshift mutations affect bases within a gene.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a physical mutagen?
options: Ultraviolet radiation
Tobacco smoke
Mustard gas
Benzene
questions.explanation: Physical mutagens include UV radiation, ionising radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays, and heat. Tobacco smoke, mustard gas and benzene are chemical mutagens.

questions.stem: A gardener works outdoors for years without sun protection and develops a skin cancer. Why would this mutation not be passed to the gardener's children?
options: It occurred in skin cells, not in cells that form gametes
UV radiation damages proteins rather than DNA
Cancer mutations are always repaired before meiosis
Skin cells contain no DNA that could be inherited
questions.explanation: Only mutations in the germline, the cells that give rise to gametes, can be inherited. A mutation in a body (somatic) cell such as a skin cell affects the person but is not passed on, even though UV does damage DNA.
